Given: effective (rms) current \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 5 \) A, \( f = 50 \) Hz (a "50 cycle" supply).
Peak value of current:
\( i_0 = \sqrt{2}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.414 \times 5 = 7.07 \) A
Current \( \frac{1}{600} \) s after it was zero: measuring t from the instant the current is zero and rising, \( i = i_0 \sin \omega t \) with \( \omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi \) rad/s.
\( \omega t = 100\pi \times \frac{1}{600} = \frac{\pi}{6} \)
\( i = 7.07 \times \sin \frac{\pi}{6} = 7.07 \times 0.5 \)
\( \therefore i = 3.535 \) A
Answer: peak current \( = 7.07 \) A; current after \( \frac{1}{600} \) s \( = 3.535 \) A.

Given: \( P = 100 \) W, \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 220 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz. A filament bulb is a purely resistive load, so its power factor is 1 and \( P = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{R} \).
(a) Resistance of the bulb:
\( R = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{P} = \frac{(220)^2}{100} = \frac{48400}{100} \)
\( \therefore R = 484\ \Omega \)
(b) rms current through the bulb:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{P}{e_{\mathrm{rms}}} = \frac{100}{220} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 0.4545 \) A
(Cross-check: \( \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{220}{484} = 0.4545 \) A, the same value.)

Given: \( C = 15.0\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 15 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 220 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz.
Capacitive reactance:
\( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{4.713 \times 10^{-3}} \)
\( \therefore X_C = 212.1\ \Omega \)
rms current:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{X_C} = \frac{220}{212.1} = 1.037 \) A
Peak current:
\( i_0 = \sqrt{2}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.414 \times 1.037 \)
\( \therefore i_0 = 1.465 \) A
If the frequency is doubled: \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \) is inversely proportional to f, so the capacitive reactance is HALVED, to \( 106.1\ \Omega \). The applied voltage is unchanged, so the current \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{X_C} \) is DOUBLED, to \( 2.074 \) A.

Given: \( L = 2 \) H, current amplitude (peak value) \( i_0 = 0.25 \) A, \( f = 60 \) Hz, \( \pi = 3.142 \).
Inductive reactance:
\( X_L = 2\pi f L = 2 \times 3.142 \times 60 \times 2 = 754.1\ \Omega \)
The current is given as a sine wave of AMPLITUDE 0.25 A, so this is the peak value and the effective (rms) current is
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{0.25}{1.414} = 0.1768 \) A
Effective potential difference across the inductor:
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = i_{\mathrm{rms}} X_L = 0.1768 \times 754.1 \)
\( \therefore e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 133.3 \) V
[Note: the textbook prints 133.4 V. The 0.07% difference is only rounding of the intermediate values; the method and the answer are the same.]

Given: \( e = 220 \sin 100\pi t \), so \( e_0 = 220 \) V and \( \omega = 100\pi \) rad/s; \( L = \frac{1}{\pi} \) H. The circuit contains inductance only.
Inductive reactance:
\( X_L = \omega L = 100\pi \times \frac{1}{\pi} = 100\ \Omega \)
Peak current:
\( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{X_L} = \frac{220}{100} = 2.2 \) A
In a purely inductive circuit the current LAGS the emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), so the instantaneous current is
\( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( \therefore i = 2.2 \sin \left( 100\pi t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \) A
An AC galvanometer (a hot-wire type meter) reads the rms value, not the peak value:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2.2}{1.414} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.555 \) A

Given: \( C = 25\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 25 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( L = 0.10 \) H, \( R = 25\ \Omega \), \( e = 310 \sin 314\, t \), so \( e_0 = 310 \) V and \( \omega = 314 \) rad/s.
Frequency:
\( f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{314}{2 \times 3.142} = 50 \) Hz
Reactances:
\( X_L = \omega L = 314 \times 0.10 = 31.4\ \Omega \)
\( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{314 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{7.85 \times 10^{-3}} = 127.4\ \Omega \)
Net reactance (the circuit is capacitance dominated, since \( X_C > X_L \)):
\( X = X_C - X_L = 127.4 - 31.4 = 95.98\ \Omega \)
Impedance:
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2} = \sqrt{(25)^2 + (95.98)^2} = \sqrt{625 + 9212} = \sqrt{9837} \)
\( \therefore Z = 99.19\ \Omega \)
Current:
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{310}{1.414} = 219.2 \) V
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{219.2}{99.19} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 2.211 \) A
Phase angle:
\( \tan\phi = \frac{X}{R} = \frac{95.98}{25} = 3.839 \)
\( \therefore \phi = \tan^{-1}(3.839) = 75.4^\circ = 1.316 \) rad
Since \( X_C > X_L \), the current LEADS the applied emf by 1.316 rad.

Given: \( C = 100\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 100 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( R = 50\ \Omega \), \( L = 0.5 \) H, \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 110 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz.
Reactances:
\( X_L = 2\pi f L = 2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.5 = 157.1\ \Omega \)
\( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 100 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{3.142 \times 10^{-2}} = 31.83\ \Omega \)
Net reactance (inductance dominated, since \( X_L > X_C \)):
\( X_L - X_C = 157.1 - 31.83 = 125.3\ \Omega \)
Impedance:
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} = \sqrt{(50)^2 + (125.3)^2} = \sqrt{2500 + 15700} = \sqrt{18200} \)
\( \therefore Z = 134.9\ \Omega \)
rms current:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{110}{134.9} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 0.8153 \) A

Given: \( R = 10\ \Omega \) in series with a capacitor, power factor \( \cos\phi = 0.5 \), \( f = 100 \) Hz. (The 80 V supply is not needed to find C.)
The power factor of a series RC circuit is \( \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z} \), so
\( Z = \frac{R}{\cos\phi} = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20\ \Omega \)
Since \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} \),
\( X_C = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2} = \sqrt{(20)^2 - (10)^2} = \sqrt{400 - 100} = \sqrt{300} \)
\( \therefore X_C = 17.32\ \Omega \)
Now \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \), so
\( C = \frac{1}{2\pi f X_C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 100 \times 17.32} = \frac{1}{10884} \)
\( \therefore C = 9.187 \times 10^{-5} \) F \( = 91.87\ \mu\mathrm{F} \)

Given: \( f = 50 \) Hz, so \( \omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi \) rad/s and the period is \( T = \frac{1}{f} = 0.02 \) s.
Measuring time from the instant the current is zero and rising,
\( i = i_0 \sin \omega t \)
The current reaches its rms value when \( i = i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} \):
\( \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} = i_0 \sin \omega t \)
\( \therefore \sin \omega t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \therefore \omega t = \frac{\pi}{4} \)
\( \therefore t = \frac{\pi}{4\omega} = \frac{\pi}{4 \times 100\pi} = \frac{1}{400} \)
\( \therefore t = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \) s
(This is \( \frac{T}{8} = \frac{0.02}{8} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \) s, i.e. one-eighth of a cycle, as expected since \( \frac{\pi}{4} \) is one-eighth of \( 2\pi \).)

Given: \( L = 101.4\ \mu\mathrm{H} = 101.4 \times 10^{-6} \) H, \( f = 1 \) MHz \( = 10^{6} \) Hz.
The frequency of LC oscillations is
\( f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \)
Squaring and rearranging for C:
\( f^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi^2 LC} \quad \therefore C = \frac{1}{4\pi^2 f^2 L} \)
\( C = \frac{1}{4 \times (3.142)^2 \times \left( 10^{6} \right)^2 \times 101.4 \times 10^{-6}} \)
\( = \frac{1}{4 \times 9.872 \times 10^{12} \times 101.4 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{4.004 \times 10^{9}} \)
\( \therefore C = 2.497 \times 10^{-10} \) F
Converting to picofarad \( \left( 1\ \mathrm{pF} = 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F} \right) \):
\( \therefore C = 249.7 \) picofarad

Given: \( C = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 10 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( V = 25 \) V, \( L = 100 \) mH \( = 0.1 \) H.
Once the battery is removed the circuit is an ideal LC loop, so the total energy is conserved. The energy is entirely electrostatic when the capacitor is fully charged and entirely magnetic when the current is maximum:
\( \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} L i_0^2 \)
\( \therefore i_0 = V \sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \)
\( = 25 \times \sqrt{\frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1}} = 25 \times \sqrt{10^{-4}} = 25 \times 10^{-2} \)
\( \therefore i_0 = 0.25 \) A
The maximum current in the coil is 0.25 A.

Given: \( C = 100\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 100 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( V = 50 \) V, maximum current \( i_0 = 5 \) A.
With the source removed the capacitor discharges through the inductance and LC oscillations are set up, so the total energy is conserved. All the electrostatic energy of the charged capacitor becomes magnetic energy of the inductor when the current is maximum:
\( \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} L i_0^2 \)
\( \therefore L = \frac{C V^2}{i_0^2} \)
\( = \frac{100 \times 10^{-6} \times (50)^2}{(5)^2} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-6} \times 2500}{25} = \frac{0.25}{25} \)
\( \therefore L = 0.01 \) H
The value of the inductance is 0.01 H (10 mH).
